text: Retrieval augmented generation connects a language model to a document store so answers are grounded in your own content rather than the model's memory.
The ingestion step loads documents from PDFs, HTML or databases, then normalises them into plain text while keeping page numbers for citation.
Chunking splits that text into pieces. Too small and a single answer is cut in half across two chunks. Too large and the real sentence drowns in noise.
Overlap between adjacent chunks means a sentence cut by a boundary still survives intact in one of the two pieces.
An embedding model turns each chunk into a dense vector. Similar meanings land near each other, which is why cosine similarity finds paraphrases.
Vector databases such as FAISS, Chroma and Pinecone store those vectors and return the nearest neighbours for a query in milliseconds.
BM25 is a sparse lexical method. It matches exact strings, which is why it finds error codes and product SKUs that embeddings blur together.
Hybrid search runs both and merges the ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion, using rank position rather than incomparable raw scores.
A cross-encoder reranker reads the query and each candidate together. Far more accurate, far too slow to run over the whole corpus.
Models attend most reliably to the beginning and the end of a long context, so a relevant chunk buried in the middle can be effectively ignored.
Faithfulness measures whether the claims in an answer are supported by the retrieved context. It catches fluent answers that invented details.
Prompt injection can arrive inside a retrieved document, which is why input filtering alone does not protect a RAG system.
To control cost, trim the context you pass. Sending ten chunks when three would do multiplies your bill and buries the right answer.
